items.lbText:
Experts say no law states third-party consent is a valid defence and call for public debate and further education

Campaigners have welcomed a call for scrutiny of consent laws by a survivor of drug-facilitated rape but said action must also focus on wider issues around sexual assault.

Joanne Young , who was drugged and raped by her husband and sexually abused by men he invited into their home, warned of “serious questions about how the law deals with consent”.

Philip Young, 50, advertised Joanne Young, his then wife, on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court heard. In fact, he had been sedating her, plunging her into an “inanimate state” in which anything could be done to her by the men who answered the adverts, jurors were told.

The former Conservative councillor pleaded guilty earlier in the year to dozens of charges of abuse against his former wife, who has waived her right to anonymity.

As four men were convicted of sexual offences against her on Thursday, Young, 49, said: “No one should be able to give [consent] on your behalf.” Her daughter, Alex Young, also called for a change in the law to make it clear that third-party consent cannot ever be used as an argument in a court of law.

Barristers and campaigners said there was no law that stated third-party consent was a valid defence as they called for a public debate and further education about consent.

Kate Parker, a criminal barrister and founder of the charity Schools Consent Project, said: “The law currently has nothing in it which allows someone to point to another person and say: ‘Because of what they told me, I believed the other person to be consenting.’ You can’t effectively outsource consent to a third party, the law has never had that within it. The Sexual Offences Act 2003 certainly doesn’t have that in it.

“What is instead happening is defence counsel in this case, and in cases like this, are pointing to a defence you can run, which is to say that the defendant genuinely and reasonably thought that the victim was consenting.”

The trial heard that the four men , who were strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her. The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.

Parker said it was right that a defendant should be able to say what was in his or her mind at the time of an alleged offence.

“I think that’s a sort of cornerstone of our law. But I hope that these arguments carry less and less traction with juries when generally there is more knowledge as to what the laws around consent are,” she said.

“I hope that as time goes by, juries become more aware and members of the public become more aware as to what the law on consent is, so no one can say: ‘Because a third party told me so and I acted on it, I thought I was legally safe.’”

Harriet Wistrich, a solicitor and the director of the Centre for Women’s Justice, said the jury in the Young case had ultimately rejected the defence.

“It should be obvious in the law that somebody can’t consent on somebody else’s behalf. But you could explicitly make it the case,” she said.

“Defence barristers should robustly defend their clients. That’s their job. But they shouldn’t overstep the mark by relying on myths and stereotypes.”

Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales, agreed the law on consent should be scrutinised. The Sexual Offences Act 2003 states: “A person consents if he agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice.”

She said: “We can look at strengthening existing laws. But really we have to get to the root of the problem, which is about the understanding of consent.

“The existing law is already clear. This is about how that law is interpreted and it is regularly misinterpreted and misapplied. That happens all the time by defendants, by barristers, by juries, and so this is highlighting a lack of understanding that consent is specific: it’s not a one-time event, it’s ongoing, it’s highly dependent on the actual situation at the time. The fact that someone is unconscious necessarily means they can’t consent.

“The other thing about these cases is that drugging someone is the opposite of consent. What is emerging from these organised drug-facilitated sexual abuse cases is a growing recognition of the attraction that some people have to a woman not being able to consent.”

Prof Miranda Horvath, the director of the Institute for Social Justice and Crime at the University of Suffolk, said incorrect beliefs about consent should be “robustly challenged”.

“It is incredibly important that people understand that legally nobody can give consent on your behalf, and this underlines the importance of clear education on consent through society, from young people right through to adults,” she said.

“Rape and serious sexual offences are a direct choice made by perpetrators, and a lack of understanding on whether a sexual partner has given consent cannot be an acceptable excuse.”

The Labour MP Jess Phillips said the government should look at whether the law should be tightened. “It is absolutely right that the government should strength-test whether there is a way of really asserting in the law that consent cannot ever come from a third party – we need to be absolutely satisfied that that is the case,” she said.

“There is an argument that while the law states that consent cannot come from a third party, we still see it being used as a defence. Perhaps if we look at tightening the law, these men would have had to plead guilty and Joanne Young would have been spared this trial.”…

Despite dodging tears in the tarmac, people are confident in city’s infrastructure – and will not worry about what has not happened yet

M ykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.

Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.

“So what if there’s a hole? The bridge hasn’t collapsed. You need to know a bit about bridge construction,” says Mykola, 65, at the wheel of a half -full afternoon bus as it clatters on its way west.

Mykola operates a marshrutka , a single deck private bus, whose drivers are famed in Kyiv mythology for being able to multi-task: chatting, smoking and collecting fares, while driving as fast as possible to take passengers from rivals.

Passengers pay 25 hryvnia (42p) in cash and typically one passenger gets the unofficial job of taking money and handing back change on behalf of the driver. It turns out this has become the Guardian’s task, in order to conduct an interview.

“It would be very difficult to destroy the bridge. It would take a huge number of missiles, and if one or two hit it, it wouldn’t be the end of the world,” Mykola continues, with behind-the-wheel speculation that is so far accurate. By lunchtime the holes have been covered up, perhaps to avoid unsettling passengers eyeing the Dnipro River below.

Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population.

Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project .

As of Friday, in an already traffic-snarled city, Kyiv’s other main road bridge, the Southern Bridge, was allowing motor traffic only from east to west. The new Podilskyi Bridge, damaged early on Friday, was similarly restricted, and the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, told people to avoid car travel after a night in which six were killed.

The Northern Bridge remains open for public transport – plus any cyclists, scooter riders and walkers willing to brave the damp late autumn weather and ignore missile and drone alerts. But below, earthworks have begun to prepare for a floating pontoon bridge, one of eight planned, in case of the worst.

Dmytro Bespalov, a transport planning expert with Kyiv’s National University of Construction and Architecture, said it was difficult to destroy a suspension bridge like the Northern. They have “a strong construction, with a lot of repairability”, meaning damage can usually be fixed. Though there are holes in the roadway, its supporting structures were so far unscathed, he added.

Russia is thought to have been aiming ballistic missiles at the supporting pylon, requiring a precise and difficult to execute attack, though that is what Ukraine did at the culmination of its complex attack on the Kerch road bridge, which was brought down after a Flamingo cruise missile struck its supporting arch .

Yet, Bespalov cautioned that Kyiv was strategically vulnerable if Russia targets the bridges with “dozens or hundreds” of missiles, because the city did not have enough bridges from before the war. “In 2021, Kyiv was in third place in Europe for congestion on the TomTom traffic index,” he said, behind Istanbul and Moscow.

Particular concern is reserved for the pontoon bridge alternative. They can bear less traffic: “It would take 20 pontoon bridges to have half the current capacity,” Bespalov said – and they are far more vulnerable to missile and drone attack. “I don’t think it would be possible to use pontoons during a red [missile] or yellow [drone] alarm” – not least because vehicles could end up in the water.

At the first busy bus stop on the eastern left bank, Nataliya, 40, and Iryna, 39, are happy to make the crossing over the Northern Bridge. They say they have long got used to the difficulties of war: “The main thing is to get through the first 24 hours at home after the initial discomfort, and then we’ll adapt,” said Nataliya, a customer service specialist.

Iryna added: “If we start to despair, that’s exactly what they want. A bridge can be built. The main thing is that when the attack comes, there are no civilians or military personnel around. It’s just concrete, that’s all. They’ll either repair it or come up with something new.”

It is a core attitude of Kyiv’s remaining residents, who are already contending with hours of electricity shortages and a lack of heating, with the full chill of winter yet to arrive. People want to deal with problems as they arise rather than worrying excessively about what may come – though it is not always easy amid the daily attacks, including a daytime raid on Thursday in which a drone exploded near the Dutch embassy .

Oleksandr, 42, a construction worker, was waiting to get across the bridge. “If the bridges are destroyed we’ll have to leave,” he conceded. If that happened, he and his wife would move to her parents’ house across the river. “I bought them a generator there; they have their own water well. We’d already dug the well during the war. They used to have gas heating, but we’ve converted it to wood-burning. We’re preparing,” he said.

items.title: Tourists are throwing fewer coins into Rome’s Trevi fountain – is €2 entry fee to blame?
items.author: Angela Giuffrida in Rome
items.content:
Charity that collects the coins says donations are down by £200,000 after a barrier was put in place to restrict access

He was well aware of the tradition among tourists of tossing a coin over their shoulder and into the waters of the baroque masterpiece, in a ritual fabled to ensure a return visit to the city or make other dreams come true.

items.lbText:
Charity that collects the coins says donations are down by £200,000 after a barrier was put in place to restrict access

When Jeff Clinton, an American visiting Rome with his wife for the first time, found a US one-cent coin on a street close to Termini train station, he knew precisely what he was going to do with it. “I’ll throw it into the Trevi fountain,” said Clinton, holding the copper coin in the palm of his hand as the couple admired the landmark.

He was well aware of the tradition among tourists of tossing a coin over their shoulder and into the waters of the baroque masterpiece, in a ritual fabled to ensure a return visit to the city or make other dreams come true.

But the only thing holding him back from partaking in the gesture was the distance: the steps towards the fountain’s sunken basin are separated by a low barrier and accessible during the day only by Rome’s residents or visitors who pay €2 (£1.64).

The fee, in place since February , has been partly blamed for taking some of the allure out of the coin-throwing tradition. The Rome unit of the church-run charity Caritas, which sweeps up the Trevi fountain’s coins, usually brings in more than €1.4m a year. But it noted a shortfall of about €200,000 between January and September compared with the same period in 2025.

“The closure of the direct access to the Trevi fountain might be a factor,” Giustino Trincia, the director of Caritas Roma, told Il Messaggero . The charity uses the donations to fund food banks and other welfare projects.

Clinton did contemplate asking someone in the basin area to throw the coin into the fountain on his behalf, but in the end slipped it back into his pocket.

The shift towards contactless payments and mobile phone wallets is also believed to have eroded Caritas’s collections.

Eric and Patty, a young couple from New York, said they might have thrown a coin, but did not have any change. Neither did they want to pay the €2 fee to get close to the basin. “It’s such a breathtaking monument, we’re happy just to take it in from here,” said Patty as they posed for selfies.

Alan and Ying, visiting Rome from Australia, did pay the fee. While they had heard that throwing coins “is what people do”, they decided not to indulge because “nobody else was really doing it”.

“I always carry cash with me because you never know when you might need it,” said Ying. “But we didn’t see anyone else doing it, so we didn’t either.”

A spokesperson for Caritas Rome told the Guardian the charity was not making any further public statements about the dwindling coin collection. The spokesperson said the collection so far this year did not take into account foreign currency coins, so the hit might not be so bad.

Still, the matter is understood to have caused friction with Rome’s council, which generated €435,194 from the access fee within the first month of its inception.

The initiative is aimed at curbing overcrowding at the monument while raising funds for the upkeep of the fountain and other Rome monuments. No further figures have been published, but with 4.4 million tourists flocking to the Trevi in 2025, the fee had been forecast to generate a tidy income for the council each year.

A team of stewards staff the ticketing system and monitor the flow of the crowd in the basin area. Nicolas Romero does shifts of seven or eight hours. He said people quite often asked him for change in order to throw a coin. “But many don’t even seem to know about the tradition,” he said. “This might also explain the decline.”

The gesture is believed to have its origins in an ancient pagan ritual offering to the water gods, although the custom of throwing coins only really took off globally after the 1954 romantic comedy film, Three Coins in the Fountain.

Victorian police allege a 17-year-old boy tasked others to carry out a series of arsons, home invasions and a mistaken identity kidnapping that resulted in the partial amputation of a victim’s finger during Melbourne’s hospitality wars.

The boy, who was arrested on Friday afternoon, allegedly communicated with the offenders under the username “Onepercent” on the encrypted communications app Signal.

He was charged on Saturday with extortion, making threats to kill, three offences of criminal damage by fire, and home invasion. He was remanded to appear in court later on Saturday.

In a statement, police said it would be alleged that Onepercent was involved in tasking an arson at a York Street, South Melbourne licensed premises on 15 April; two home invasions and a kidnapping four days apart in Springvale later that month; and two arson attacks during March at a Williamstown ice-cream store and a car in Moonee Ponds.

The boy was arrested at a house in the Moonee Ponds region, in Melbourne’s north-west, police said.

It is alleged a trafficable quantity of cocaine, three phones and cash were seized during the arrest.

Police allege that when the mistaken identity kidnapping occurred at the Springvale property on 22 April, a 34-year-old victim received serious injuries to his lower body and the partial amputation of one of his fingers.

It is alleged the fire at Capriccio Gelateria in Williamstown on 22 March caused $600,000 worth of damage and endangered the lives of residents at the property upstairs.

On 16 November, police appealed for more information about the person behind the Onepercent user name.

“We need the public’s assistance to identify the user of this handle,” Det Insp Graham Banks said at the time.

“There will be people in the wider organised crime network and in our community who will have intimate knowledge of who this person is.

“We are hopeful that those people may now be in a position to come forward and speak to police.”

items.content:

items.lbText:
Survivors recount rivers red with blood and burning nearby villages serving as an urgent warning to flee their homes

Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next.

In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee.

What happened during the escape from Myanmar – a journey through forests and over hills and rivers while being battered by monsoon rains – was a key part of the ruling made this week in The Hague that Myanmar had carried out a genocide against the Rohingya .

The international court of justice (ICJ) said it was not enough to say they had faced ethnic cleansing when soldiers had also killed those trying to escape – Myanmar was trying to destroy the group as a people.

Stories of that violence in 2017, of organised mass killing, sexual attacks and the complete destruction of their villages, came with the refugees who arrived in neighbouring Bangladesh , eventually numbering more than 700,000 and settling in what has become the world’s largest refugee camp.

For months, they would arrive from places such as Tula Toli , where thousands were rounded up, killed and buried in mass graves. In other villages, men were captured and killed by the security forces.

Many survivors had escaped an attack on their own village, only to watch their relatives being killed in the villages where they had sought safety.

Almost a decade later, the majority of Rohingya who arrived in 2017 remain in the refugee camps, joining those who had already been there since the early 1990s, having escaped previous military operations and ever-increasing persecution.

The ICJ ruling has come at a particularly harsh time for Rohingya refugees, in a year in which hundreds have died at sea trying to escape the refugee camps, and in which countries such as Malaysia and India have spoken about returning the Rohingya to Myanmar.

Rohingya campaigners are hoping that this ruling will put an end to that.

Rohingya refugees still live in fragile shelters made of bamboo and tarpaulin sheets. They are denied the right to leave the camps, to work or to seek education.

Below are some of the stories from Rohingya who arrived in Bangladesh in 2017, having escaped Tula Toli and the surrounding area.

Sitting in the background, almost unnoticed as Momtaz Begum recollected how Myanmar forces had killed her husband and children and then raped her in front of her lone surviving child, was a woman who seemed to know every word of the story.

It was not because she had heard it before. Dildar Begum had experienced exactly the same violence as her sister had, in their village, Tula Toli.

In fact, they had for months believed each other dead until they discovered that they had both made it to Bangladesh and lived in different parts of the camp.

Each had only one surviving daughter, both of whom had similar scars along the back of their heads.

Twice previously Anwara Begum had lived as a refugee in Bangladesh. Once as a child in 1978 and then again in the early 1990s, as a young mother who lost her son to a respiratory disease during a rainy season spent in a flimsy tent.

When she was forced to return to Myanmar, though the persecution she fled there had not stopped, Anwara swore to herself that she would never become a refugee again.

She broke that oath when she saw the river by her village filled with bodies floating from Tula Toli.

Her husband first pulled from the river as many bodies as he could to bury and then they gathered some belongings and headed westwards to the River Naf – the border with Bangladesh.

To cross, she handed over all the gold she owned, equal to US $200 (£150), to a Bangladeshi boatman.

Elderly people were not spared the Myanmar military’s attacks. Like so many others, Nur Alam had to be carried on the shoulders of his children on his journey to Bangladesh.

His 10-year-old grandson, Mamoon, held his hand. Once in the camp, they stuck to each other.

Alam’s arrival in Bangladesh was his fourth time being a refugee there. He was first expelled from Myanmar – known as Burma until 1989 – during military operations in the 1950s when Bangladesh was not yet an independent country.

items.title: ‘A new record for entertainment’: Grand Theft Auto VI sales hit $3.8bn on first day of release, developer says
items.author: Guardian staff and agencies
items.content:

items.lbText:
The announcement from Rockstar Games would mean GTA VI has already earned more than the entire box office run of the highest-grossing film of all time

Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day , publisher Rockstar Games has announced, calling it the biggest launch for any entertainment product in history.

The worldwide figure was based on company estimates through the end of the day Thursday, the day the game launched. Rockstar said also it had sold 32.5m units of the game on prerelease, setting a record across platforms.

“We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder, said in a statement.

The company said the sales set “a new record for entertainment across any medium … becoming the biggest entertainment launch in history.”

The figure is nearly five times the roughly $800m that predecessor Grand Theft Auto V attracted during its first 24 hours in 2013 .

It also exceeds the entire box office run of Avengers: Endgame, which became the highest-grossing film of all time last month at about $2.9bn worldwide after a rerelease pushed it past Avatar.

The game went on sale Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, launching first in New Zealand and rolling out market by market as each reached midnight local time.

The release quickly became a global phenomenon, generating more social media posts than this year’s World Cup, according to monitoring platform Visibrain.

Critics praised the game, which has a score of 99 on review aggregator Metacritic.

Rockstar said that made it the highest-rated game ever.

Like its predecessors, “GTA VI” is an open-world action game in which players roam freely through a sprawling city, stealing cars, pulling off heists and carrying out missions for criminal gangs.

Its busy streets, neon-lit nightlife and beaches are rendered in striking detail, and non-player characters go about their lives whether or not the player is involved.

While critics have raved about the game, it has also prompted real-world warnings from authorities .

With the game’s release on Thursday, police departments across the US reminded people that the car thefts, reckless driving, violence and other criminal mayhem depicted in the blockbuster title should not be re-enacted on the country’s streets.

There is insufficient evidence supporting a scientific causal link between violent video games and violent behaviour, according to the American Psycyhological Association. Nonetheless, several police departments took to the internet with warnings – and even jokes – aimed at keeping GTA VI’s lawlessness firmly in the virtual world.

The Atlanta police department delivered one of the clearest messages in a social media post.

“GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is!” the department warned. “Don’t confuse virtual entertainment with real-life decisions.”

With the Associated Press and Agence France-Presse

items.lbText:
Verdict in case against former Uber driver Jonathan Rinderknecht comes after first trial ended with hung jury

The 30-year-old accused of sparking the deadly Palisades fire in Los Angeles was found guilty of two federal arson charges in a Friday verdict that came months after his first trial concluded with a hung jury.

For two weeks, a fresh batch of jurors listened to prosecutors mount their case against Jonathan Rinderknecht.

They argued the former Uber driver was responsible for the January 2025 wildfire, which claimed 12 lives and devastated the Pacific Palisades, an affluent enclave on the California coast.

Rinderknecht, in prosecutors’ account, used a lighter to set a brush fire in the hillside area. The state cast him as a disgruntled young man who sought retribution against the world for personal gripes, including failed romances, and perceived societal injustices like wealth inequality.

Firefighters suppressed the so-called Lachman brush fire last January, but its embers simmered underground, before being swept by powerful winds and erupting above ground into the Palisades inferno that destroyed thousands of homes and businesses.

Rinderknecht had maintained his innocence, pleading not guilty to the revised charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.

For the retrial, jurors were instructed explicitly to not consider the adequacy of the fire department’s response to the Lachman and Palisades blaze. The department has faced criticism for failing to fully extinguish the Lachman fire that eventually reignited.

The note came after some of the first trial’s jurors were wary of pinning the blame squarely on Rinderknecht, citing the fire department’s past actions. Of that deadlocked panel, two voted for guilty, while 10 others were not convinced.

Rinderknecht’s defense team also doubled down during the retrial on an alternative explanation for the Palisades fire, suggesting the initial brush blaze was ignited by fireworks.

Prosecutors dismissed the theory as “baseless” in a court filing where they raised concern over the reliability and late introduction of a defense witness, whose testimony would reference stains at a private residence that supposedly indicated fireworks had been discharged.

Rinderknecht will be sentenced on 17 March.

items.lbText:
Exclusive: Independent candidate Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s cards instruct people to vote in a way that would benefit Liberal party

Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast

The Victorian Greens are seeking an urgent injunction from the supreme court to stop an independent candidate distributing how-to-vote cards that allegedly mimic the party’s branding and urge people to preference it last.

As prepoll opened on Wednesday morning, Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s campaign team handed out how-to-vote cards that used the minor party’s colour scheme, font and triangle logo with the banner “Vote 1 Green Values”.

The card instructed people to vote in a way that would ultimately benefit the Liberal party. It asked voters to give their first preference to Finnigan followed by an Animal Justice party candidate, another independent candidate and then the Liberals in fourth place.

The Greens are determined to win back the ultra-marginal seat it lost to the Liberals at a February 2025 byelection with a 1.3% margin. Labor is running an open ticket in Prahran, which the Greens fear could deprive it of the preference votes it needs .

On Wednesday afternoon, the Greens state director, Martin Shield, requested Finnigan immediately stop distributing the material and threatened to take legal action if an undertaking was not given to do so in less than two hours.

Finnigan agreed to the request and produced an amended how-to-vote card within hours that included different colours with a revised banner that said “Vote 1 Trans Greens Values”.

“Due to legal threats from the Greens party, I confirm that I am not an endorsed Greens party candidate,” a disclaimer on Finnigan’s revised how-to-vote card said.

But the changes did not satisfy the Greens. On Friday afternoon, the party’s lawyers lodged papers in the supreme court.

At an initial hearing on Friday night, the Greens’ lawyer, Adam McBeth, alleged people handing out Finnigan’s material at prepoll wore shirts with the exact shade of green as worn by genuine Greens party volunteers.

McBeth alleged Finnigan’s team stood next to Greens party volunteers and Greens placards. The party argues voters at prepoll were deliberately misled.

“There is no other reason for an independent candidate who has an infinite range of colours and styles to choose from to so closely mimic the Greens, including the way people paid to hand out were dressed and where they were directed to stand,” McBeth said.

Finnigan, who was self-represented, said they had gone above and beyond to quickly make changes to their initial how-to-vote card and accused the Greens of using “legal manoeuvres” to stop them campaigning.

“It is my belief that they don’t want me to hand out on Saturday, which will be one of the busiest days of prepoll,” Finnigan said.

Finnigan told the court that they did not have enough money to print new cards. They said their campaign team had not been instructed to stand next to the Greens at prepoll.

“I am someone who holds Greens values, of course I am going to have some kind of green shirt,” Finnigan said.

“The honest reason I went for that colour of green is because the colour is called Irish green and I am of Irish background. That’s why I went for it. I just like the sound of Irish green.”

On Friday evening, after the supreme court action was lodged, the Victorian Election Commission (VEC) accepted Finnigan’s subsequent how-to-vote card and published it online.

Justice John Watson said the first how-to-vote card “looked like a pretty deliberate attempt to pass yourself off as a Greens candidate”, but he adjourned the matter until 3pm on Saturday to hear testimony from the VEC.

A decision on whether to grant an injunction will be made on Sunday morning.

Finnigan became Victoria’s first openly transgender councillor in 2023 when they were elected to the Colac Otway shire council after a countback. They resigned from the council in October 2024.

The former Labor field campaigner founded the Restore Democracy Sack Dan Andrews party in 2022. They unsuccessfully contested an upper house seat for the party, securing 1% of first preference votes.

After working in the offices of Labor ministers during the 2014 state campaign, Finnigan became a whistleblower in the so-called Red Shirts scandal, which saw taxpayer funds used to pay electorate officers campaigning for Labor.

Finnigan’s campaign Facebook page carrying an authorisation message describes them as a “Green Independent” and contains attack ads against the minor party.

items.lbText:
The president appeared to put Vance and Rubio through their paces as potential successors, though Stephen Miller unexpectedly stole the spotlight

“Which of you shall we say doth love us most?”

The ageing King Lear’s question to his daughters, expecting them to compete for his favour and carve up his kingdom, hovered in the White House press briefing room on Friday.

There at the lectern stood Donald “Lear” Trump. Behind him stood his potential heirs, JD “Goneril” Vance and Marco “Regan” Rubio, and to the side sat Trump’s favourite offspring, Stephen “Cordelia” Miller (more of him later). As for Lear’s Fool, the choices were endless.

Ostensibly this was a press conference to trumpet the president’s trip in Asia, but in practice everyone knew it was the first audition for the 2028 presidential election (and boy, is Trump going to enjoy turning the race into a contest for his approval). Vance is widely expected to seek the crown, though it was Rubio who came out on top in the latest Emerson College national poll .

In a jam-packed room, Trump stood centre stage as if hosting The Apprentice all over again. Behind him were the two contenders expressing their aspirations through matching suits, matching Maga red ties, matching US flag pins and matching leather shoes.

The first trial: could Vance and Rubio stand still for 90 minutes without rolling their eyes, yawning or silently mouthing “Kill me!” to the press? Could they force Trump’s word salad down their throats and look as if they were enjoying it? Even when the boss was rambling at length about potholes?

“When you fix a pothole”, began one detour by the octogenarian president. “I don’t want to bore you – they’ll say, oh, he rambled, he rambled terribly. I don’t ramble. I don’t ramble at all, but when you fix a pothole, you have brand new asphalt against old white asphalt that doesn’t look good, but at least you don’t ruin your car, but these roads were flawless …”

But first, the whole thing got off to a strange start. Trump appeared at the podium and remarked: “That’s a big, big a crowd. I’ve never seen this before,” but reporters crammed in the room could barely hear him above the whoosh of an air conditioning unit. An engineer tweaked the sound, but it only gave Trump’s voice an eerie echo.

Had the gremlins that grounded flights and frozen banking sites finally reached the White House? So much for America the hi-tech superpower. Eventually order was restored, though not necessarily in Trump’s brain.

He was evidently flattered by the media comparing his trilateral summit with the leaders of China and Russia to the Yalta meeting between Winston Churchill, Franklin Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin (he did not say which of the three he identified with, though critics could take a guess). Like a gushing teenager, Trump was so thrilled that Chinese president Xi Jinping had come to the airport to greet him, that he mentioned it twice (“He didn’t meet Sleepy Joe with the plane, that I can tell you.”)

The US, Russia and China hold 92% of global nuclear power, he noted, which gave him an excuse to bring up his uncle John Trump , an electrical engineer and former Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor. “A member of my family spent his life at MIT who they say is now the greatest professor in the history of MIT, so I have great understanding of- I guess maybe genetically I’m blessed,” Trump riffed.

At that remark Rubio could resist no longer. A smile spread across his lips and he shot a look at Vance, who felt obliged to smile back. We’re not laughing at you, we’re laughing with you, Mr President.

Indeed, Rubio had been the more fidgety of the pair. As Trump chuntered on, the secretary of state had shifted from foot to foot, fiddled with his tie, played with his lower lip, touched up his hair and given the odd wry smile. Vance, meanwhile, hid behind his beard and miasma of smugness.

But then, at last, came the moment for Lear’s daughters to make their public declarations of love. Vance went up the lectern and pointed out that he had stayed in Washington rather than joining the trip, comparing himself to Macaulay Culkin’s character in Home Alone – a child who is accidentally left behind at Christmas as his family rushes to catch a flight to Paris. “I missed you, sir,” he said to Trump, before praising the president for “securing historic trade deals” and reorganising the global economy to benefit the American worker and economy.

Not bad, but a little wonky. Marco, you’re up next. The secretary of state took aim at the critics who accused Trump of cosying up to dictators at the expense of Democrats, raising his eyebrows and shaking his fist: “These three countries possess the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet. The idea that these three leaders should not engage on a regular basis is not just absurd, it’s dangerous.”

Trump began taking reporters’ questions. One young whippersnapper posed a question that will be asked many times over the next two years. “Because you have the vice-president, the secretary of state right behind you, I’m curious which of them do you think would make a better president after you?”

Trump swatted it aside without answering. Vance remained stony faced. Rubio smiled knowingly.

The same reporter put Vance in an uncomfortable spot by asking about his post-midterm tweet. “Would you argue that the war in Iran was worth it to lose the Senate?” The vice-president agreed with the goal of Iran not getting a nuclear weapon but added carefully: “I think the president is the one who makes the decision and the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States.”

In other words, I hate this war and would never have started it but I have to back the boss. Expect a lot more of this needle-threading in the upcoming campaign.…

items.lbText:
A public vigil and celebration of life honor the civil rights activist and co-founder of United Farm Workers union

Hundreds of people came out to honor and celebrate the life and legacy of the California civil rights activist Dolores Huerta at a celebration-of-life event Friday in Bakersfield.

Huerta’s daughter Lori de Leon thanked attendees for their support during her mother’s passing, highlighting the widespread tributes and communities gathering in her honor.

Huerta’s casket was escorted inside the Dignity Health arena for the interfaith memorial service as Mariachi Lindas Mexicanas played next to it.

Huerta, a feminist icon who co-founded the United Farm Workers (UFW) in 1962, died on 28 October aged 96.

Attenders came from all over California to pay their respects. Rosa de la Cruz, a 44-year-old farm worker who lives in Tulare, about an hour north of Bakersfield, said she wanted to pay her respects in person.

The world-renowned labor rights leader and activist means “a great deal”, de la Cruz said, “because if it hadn’t been for her, there wouldn’t be many benefits for the people who work in the fields.”

The week was filled with events dedicated to Huerta’s memory, her courage, resilience and her impact on the community.

On Monday, Huerta was honored in Sacramento by state government officials including Monique Limón, the senate president pro tempore, Robert Rivas, the assembly speaker, Xavier Becerra, the California governor-elect, and community leaders in a historic ceremony.

Huerta became the first female, first Latino and first non-elected leader to lie in honor at the state capitol. Her casket was escorted in after a march organized by local unions.

“Our mother devoted her entire life to fighting injustice and lifting up communities too often left out and treated unfairly,” said Huerta’s family. “As a lifelong organizer, her activism has been a source of inspiration and empowerment for people around the world.”

For more than six decades, Huerta spearheaded historic boycotts, fought tirelessly for farm workers’ rights, women’s equality and environmental justice, and coined the enduring national rally cry, “ ¡Sí, se puede! ”

Huerta has received numerous honors including the Eleanor Roosevelt Human Rights Awards. In 2012, Barack Obama awarded Huerta the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor.

The two-day tribute started on Thursday evening with a public rosary and vigil in Bakersfield, where she had lived since 1990.

Friday’s interfaith memorial service and celebration of life began with an opening blessing by Aztec dancers. There were performances from music groups Los Lobos, Ozomatli, Las Cafeteras, Nancy Sanchez and Trio los Dados. Rob Bonta, the California attorney general, was among the speakers on Friday.

“Dolores Huerta is irreplaceable and her loss is something I think people are still, including me, getting our heads around,” Bonta said. “To the world, she is an icon and a giant and a legend. For me, she was also a friend and a mentor and a counselor. Someone I texted with and called and sought advice from and leaned on as I launched my career and had my career in elected public office.”

“Her loss is immeasurable. She is irreplaceable but she leaves a legacy of fighting for justice,” Bonta said.

Ten of Huerta’s adult children took the stage to share personal anecdotes about Huerta’s life, emphasizing her skills as an organizer, political strategist and motivational speaker. Her children recounted her dedication to social justice, her love for jazz, and her humility despite her significant contributions.

“While there is much to celebrate in our recent victories, there is still so much work to be done,” said Huerta’s daughter Camila Chavez. “People may expect us to fill her shoes, but she is going to be buried with her shoes. Like Zapata said: ‘I’d rather live on my feet than die on my knees.’ It’s going to take all of us here to fill those shoes.”

Her legacy will continue through the work and empowering mission of the Dolores Huerta Foundation. In 2003, Huerta founded the grassroots community organization to create leadership opportunities for community members, while organizing underserved communities, and pursuing social justice.

Huerta kept on working even as a nonagenarian, dedicating her life as an organizer.

In the Central valley, Huerta supported minorities to run for office to make a difference at the local, state and federal level. In a 2022 speech, Huerta encouraged new US citizens to fulfill their civic responsibilities, especially voting.

For her 94th birthday, Huerta asked people to help her celebrate by getting others involved in elections either by talking to somebody about voting and about registering to vote.

Huerta urged uninsured Latinos and Californians to enroll in health coverage with the passage of the Affordable Care Act partnering with Covered California to spread the message. Huerta also had several schools named after her throughout the state. Last year, Huerta joined Central valley educators to demand David Valadao, a US representative from California, defend funding for schools.

Thom Tillis move comes after Michael LoSapio, nominated for Cisa role, told hearing ‘I don’t believe it was an attack’

Senator Thom Tillis, the outgoing North Carolina Republican who is due to be replaced by a Democrat, has reportedly blocked a confirmation vote on Donald Trump’s nominee to lead a key US cybersecurity agency, Michael LoSapio, after he denied during a hearing that the Capitol was attacked on January 6 2021.

Tillis, who declined to run for re-election and after repeated clashes with Trump’s, confirmed to HuffPost on Friday that he has placed a hold on LoSapio’s nomination to serve as a director of the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency (Cisa). His block on the nomination will prevent it from being included in a package of nominees to be voted on next month, before the Republicans lose their majority in the Senate.

At his Senate confirmation hearing on Thursday, LoSapio, the chief information security officer for Palantir, a technology firm founded by JD Vance’s mentor, Peter Thiel, was asked by senator Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat: “Was there an attack on the Capitol of January 6 2021?”

After initially replying, “I don’t know,” LoSapio said: “No, I don’t believe it was an attack.”

Tillis told the Hill that the question of whether a mob of Trump supporters attacked the US Capitol in an attempt to overturn Joe Biden’s 2020 victory was not open for debate.

“It’s binary,” Tillis told the outlet. “The minute you pretend like it didn’t exist or you can’t even acknowledge it, I don’t have any time because it’s not a very thoughtful person.”

The agency LoSapio was nominated by Trump to lead, Cisa, plays a role in protecting US elections infrastructure from hacking.

The week after the 2020 election, as Trump falsely claimed that count had been rigged, Cisa was one of a number of federal agencies with oversight of election infrastructure to issue a statement calling the election “the most secure in American history” and noting that there was “no evidence that any voting system deleted or lost votes, changed votes, or was in any way compromised.”

After he returned to the White House last year, Trump signed an April 2025 presidential memorandum directing executive offices to take steps to address supposed “risks from Chris Krebs”, who led Cisa in 2020.

“Krebs, through CISA, falsely and baselessly denied that the 2020 election was rigged and stolen, including by inappropriately and categorically dismissing widespread election malfeasance and serious vulnerabilities with voting machines,” Trump’s memorandum claimed.

items.lbText:
Labor says allowing mine to increase production reflects ‘gravity of situation facing hundreds of workers’ – but critics call it ‘unprecedented and dangerous’

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

The New South Wales government has passed special legislation to allow a coalmine in the Hunter Valley to increase production by 32% in its final act of parliament before the March state election, in which the region will be a key battleground for One Nation.

After a marathon session in the legislative council on Friday, the Minns government and the Coalition voted at 1.36am on Saturday morning to allow the Mount Pleasant mine to increase its annual extraction rate from 12.5MT to 16.5MT until 2032.

At the start of debate, the resources minister, Courtney Houssos, told the upper house “this is a unique bill applying to unique circumstances”.

“Taking the decision to intervene in the way we have is not an easy one, but it is an important one,” she said. “And it does reflect the gravity of the situation facing hundreds of workers and their families in the Hunter.”

The legislation has drawn outcry from legal and anti-corruption experts, climate groups, crossbenchers and civil liberties organisations, after the high court ruled last month that an approval for an expansion that would increase the mine’s annual output to 21MT until 2048 was invalid.

In a 3-2 split ruling, the high court found the state’s Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to properly consider imposing conditions to minimise greenhouse gas emissions that would be generated by the mine when the coal is sold and burned overseas.

Despite saying he would not bypass the court’s decision, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, subsequently announced the legislation , claiming it would save 400 jobs ahead of Christmas.

On Friday, the government and Coalition used their numbers to block almost 200 amendments to the bill sought by the Greens, who called the legislation “exceptional and unprecedented and dangerous”. Animal Justice party MLC Emma Hurst also opposed the bill.

“Labor describes the circumstances as exceptional, says this case is unique, and assures the public that other companies shouldn’t expect the same treatment,” the Greens climate spokesperson, Sue Higginson, told the parliament.

“But a political assurance offers no protection against the precedent being set.”

She accused the premier of being motivated by a desire to withstand a threat from One Nation to Labor seats in the Hunter.

“It’s very clear to us why Chris Minns has gone here, and that is because we’re really on the eve of an election, and One Nation is right now his threat,” she said at a press conference on Thursday.

The Hunter region, the centre of NSW’s coalmining industry, is emerging as a key battleground at the March 2027 state election. The One Nation NSW upper house candidate and former coalminer Stuart Bonds contested the Labor-held federal seat of Hunter in 2025, winning 41% of the two-candidate preferred vote. The party’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, is running in the Labor-held lower house seat of Cessnock .

Higginson told the upper house that in bringing the bill, the government had turned its back on the advice of the state’s Net Zero Commission, which has said further coalmine expansions are incompatible with meeting legislated emissions reduction targets.

“But who seems to care any more? What does the rule of law matter when [the premier] visits the Hunter and decides he needs to do something for someone so that he can remain somewhat popular in his own mind?” she said.

The Coalition, which supported the bill, said it was “about people”.

“It’s about the hundreds of workers at MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant mine who, since the high court handed down its decision in October, have been left wondering whether they will still have a job in the new year,” Nationals MLC Sarah Mitchell said.

She said “losing hundreds of jobs in one go would completely devastate the Hunter region”.

The legislation ties consent for the mine expansion to a jobs guarantee protecting workers at the mine. Data provided to the government by the mine for the jobs guarantee, which covers more than 720 workers, is subject to an independent audit.

At a press conference on Wednesday, Minns said the legal proceedings would return to the land and environment court for consideration, but it would be “a tragedy if, in the meantime, that community effectively shut down as a result of this decision”.

“Most of the workers from Mount Pleasant live in Muswellbrook, and if the mine closed, the unemployment rate would jump by 5% just in that small town,” he said, speaking alongside workers at the mine and the Mining and Energy Union, which has welcomed the legislation.

In a report published on Tuesday, the parliament’s legislation review committee found the Mount Pleasant bill would “effectively undermine” proceedings that were still before the land and environment court and “would undermine procedural fairness” by removing avenues for legal challenge.

That report also highlighted concerns with a so-called Henry VIII clause that the barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson warned this week posed a “serious corruption risk” to the state.

The clause, allowing the resources minister of the day to override state laws as they apply to the Mount Pleasant development, was amended by the government in the lower house. Following the amendments, it cannot be used to prevent development from being subject to Icac investigations or to change the permitted coal production limit.

The Nature Conservation Council of NSW said the government had been “embarrassed into amending its own coalmining bill”, while the Greens said the amendments did not go far enough to constrain the power any resources minister might hold under the clause.…

items.title: French police officers found guilty of racist assault on black music producer
items.author: Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
items.content:

Three French police officers who beat a black music producer they said was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic have been found guilty of intentional, racist violence.

The brutal assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, was caught on security cameras in his building in 2020 and triggered outrage in France over police brutality. The trial this month was considered a turning point for the recognition of racist violence.

items.lbText:
Beating of Michel Zecler in 2020 sparked outrage over police brutality after it was caught on security cameras

Three French police officers who beat a black music producer they said was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic have been found guilty of intentional, racist violence.

The brutal assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, was caught on security cameras in his building in 2020 and triggered outrage in France over police brutality. The trial this month was considered a turning point for the recognition of racist violence.

The officers were sentenced to between one and two years in prison, with additional years suspended. They were banned for life from serving in the police.

The officers had stopped Zecler outside his Paris music studio on 21 November 2020, accusing him of failing to wear a mandatory face mask. They pushed him into the entrance of his office and violently beat him in an assault recorded by his studio’s security cameras .

Zecler sustained about 30 punches and truncheon blows to the face and body over a five-minute period, according to the investigation. He was left with craniofacial trauma, a wound to the lip and scalp, and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon, leaving him unable to work for 45 days.

Zecler told the court the officers used a racist slur against him on several occasions during the beating. He said the attack had “completely devastated him” and had left a lasting physical and psychological impact.

The three officers, Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Pierre Plantier, 37, and Philippe Tondeux, 50, were found guilty of breaking into Zecler’s studio and committing intentional violence in a group. The judges decided racism was an aggravating factor in the attack.

The officers were also found guilty of forgery after they tried to cover up their actions by falsifying an official police report saying Zecler had been violent towards them. The police used that report to accuse Zecler of attacking them and trying to grab one of their weapons, but the video footage did not back up the claims, showing he was not violent.

The state prosecutor said that without the CCTV footage, the false police report on Zecler could have resulted in him being convicted of attacking a police officer in what would have been a serious miscarriage of justice.

The state prosecutor, who asked not to be named in the media, told the court the case had caused “immense harm to Michel Zecler but also to society as a whole”.

She said the officers had “betrayed” their uniform. She told the judges: “I ask you to believe Michel Zecler, to recognise him as a victim of these racist insults.”

The three police officers, who had not realised their attack was being recorded on security cameras, had apologised in court for beating Zecler, but denied racism.

Zecler’s lawyers and supporters said the trial had shone a spotlight on police violence in France , which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions say is limited to isolated cases. Many members of the public who had come to support Zecler and watch the trial said it was an important moment in confronting institutionalised racism.

One of Zecler’s lawyers, Serge Money, said while summing up the case: “A verdict can force a society to really look at an injustice that up until now had been tolerated, minimised, and I dare to use the word: institutionalised.”

He said: “The Zecler trial is the trial of impunity, for all those who before him and after him will experience the same thing.”

Money told the court: “I want you to give voice to all those who didn’t have security cameras, and to all those who were not believed.”

Nine young performers who had been rehearsing in the basement at Zecler’s studio had been violently arrested when they came to assist Zecler.

Their lawyer, Seydi Ba, told the court that France needed to know how “police violence, lies and racism” would be considered by a court.

items.lbText:
President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi

Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.

He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.

“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.

With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”

He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”

Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.

“I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”

He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.

“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.

Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”

And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

items.lbText:
Nasdaq erases 2026 gains and Asian markets record worst week since 2020 as investors question huge sums being poured into AI build-out

Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?

Anthropic’s shares fell at the start of its second day of trading, as its record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.

As they dropped, the wider stock market fell with them, with the Nasdaq Composite erasing all its gains for 2026. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 briefly entered correction territory.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by as much as 12% on Friday. They dropped to $85.12, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, knocking 2.9% off the value of the Nasdaq share index, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. The broader S&P 500 share index fell 1.66% in morning trading in New York.

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled -12% to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO .

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI build out.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”

Nvidia shares fell by 7% after California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.

Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.

Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

items.lbText:
Jamie Dimon says he is ‘setting an example’ in seeking to claw back Labour’s increase in surcharge, from 3% to 6%

Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair.

Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”.

The bank surcharge is to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. It was unclear how JP Morgan , which employs 23,000 people in the UK, would make up for the extra cost.

In comments first reported by the Financial Times, citing people who attended the event, Dimon said he would set an example in making up for the added costs, and that the decision was “more in sorrow” than in anger.

Dimon has repeatedly lobbied Labour against raising taxes on banks, and suggested in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn tower in the Canary Wharf district of London that is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters.

Shortly after the chancellor, John Healey, announced the policy during his inaugural budget in October, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian that plans for the 279,000 sq metre (3m sq ft) building were still going ahead. But the bank also said at the time that the policy “lacks principle” for singling the sector out, adding that it operated in a “highly competitive global marketplace”.

JP Morgan also has a sprawling campus in Bournemouth, where it employs more than 5,300 staff who process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported fears that the advance of artificial intelligence could put their jobs at risk.

Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, and the separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets, which is set for the temporary rise. JP Morgan, the biggest bank in the US, expected to pay £120m more in taxes because of the increase, the FT reported.

Bank share prices rallied after Healey’s October announcement because the increase was less than many people in the industry had expected. The chancellor said at the time that he was “looking to our banks to help fund breathing space for British families”.

items.lbText:
Sally-Anne Bowen was found guilty of having sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the 1980s

Police are searching for a missing chemistry teacher convicted of sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the late 1980s after she did not turn up to her sentencing hearing.

Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, was not found at her Hemel Hempstead home by Metropolitan police officers after her failure to attend Harrow crown court in north London on Friday, where a warrant was issued for her arrest.

Bowen’s barrister, Mark Kimsey, told the court she was in contact with solicitors on Thursday and had engaged with a pre-sentence report, adding there had been “concerns as to her welfare due to the content of the messages” from her.

The former teacher, who was in her 20s when she had sex with one pupil up to 30 times and kissed a second boy when they were aged about 14 to 15, was convicted in August of seven counts of indecent assault and granted bail before her sentencing.

Judge Karim Ezzat issued a warrant for her arrest, which he said was “not backed by bail”.

Neelam Gomersall, prosecuting, said Bowen’s partner of 36 years, Darren Scotchbrook, was at the home address when officers arrived, but Bowen was not.

Gomersall earlier told the court there was “no evidence” that Bowen could not attend the sentencing, and that information from her partner was “suggestive of refusal rather than inability” to attend.

The Met said: “On Friday 20 November, officers were made aware that a 65-year-old woman had failed to appear at Harrow crown court for sentencing. A warrant has been issued for her arrest, and inquiries to locate her are ongoing.”

The trial heard that Bowen was in her mid-20s when she taught at Christ’s College in Finchley, north London.

Jurors heard she had worn short, tight skirts and flirted in class, with one former pupil comparing her behaviour to “a Sabrina Carpenter video”.

One victim told jurors he had had sex with her “about 20 or 30 times” over several months, considered her his girlfriend and kept it secret. He said it had led to “the destruction of my education”.

The second victim described spending lunchtimes with Bowen in a cafe, where he was “goaded” into kissing her by other boys and recalled touching her breasts.

Bowen denied the allegations as “total fabrication” and claimed a medical condition made sex difficult and painful. She denied flirting, saying: “I didn’t flirt with students, I was just friendly.” Defending her clothes, she said she “wasn’t going to dress like Margaret Thatcher”.

items.lbText:
Dwain Hall was convicted of stabbing Sonia Exelby, a music teacher who prosecutors say suffered from mental illness

A Florida mechanic has been found guilty of stabbing to death a British music teacher, whom he convinced to travel to the United States.

Dwain Hall, an auto repair and tow truck driver, groomed 32-year-old Sonia Exelby from Portsmouth, England, on a fetish website before luring her to the US.

Hall had pleaded not guilty to the charges of kidnap and first-degree murder.

At trial, jurors heard from several witnesses, most of them law enforcement officials, who detailed Hall’s email, phone records, social media accounts and other records to trace his movements after Exelby travelled from the UK to meet him.

Exelby’s disappearance from her home sparked an international investigation. Prosecutors this week described how she suffered from mental illness. Investigators said that Exelby had traveled to Florida after posting online about wanting someone to end her life.

Hall’s arrest affidavit said that Exelby had previously expressed suicidal thoughts and investigators alleged that Hall knew about her struggles and used that vulnerability to bring her to Florida, the Ocala Starbanner reported .

The authorities said Exelby boarded a flight to the US seemingly with an intention “to be possibly sexually abused, tortured and murdered by unknown individuals living in the United States”.

After Exelby traveled to the US in October 2025, authorities say Hall picked her up from the Gainesville airport in central Florida .

He drove her to an Airbnb rental, where investigators later found evidence they say connected him to her disappearance and death, including transactions on her bank cards and a video of Exelby on Hall’s cellphone.

According to the Times , Junior Barrett, Hall’s attorney, argued that Exelby took her own life. “She came here with the intention of dying, she thought she was worthless, useless, a burden on other people,” he said in his closing statement.

“This isn’t a question about what porn he likes. You can disagree with him about what he likes, but the case can’t be decided on you not liking his lifestyle. The fact he did not stop her from killing herself does not make it murder.”

Prosecutor Amy Beth Berndt said jurors should use their “common sense”. She added that Hall targeted Exelby for her mental illness and killed her for his sadistic pleasure.

Berndt said Exelby “was beautiful. She was kind and she was deeply loved by everyone who knew her. And she also suffered from mental illness for most of her life. She should be alive today.”

She added: “No one could save her from the defendant, the ‘Alpha Sadist’. He took advantage of a severely depressed, mentally ill woman who was incapable of making any rational decisions.”

After the verdict was read, Exelby’s brother Barry Wilton said: “This last year has been one of the hardest of our lives. Losing our dear sister Sonia has had a profound impact on me and my entire family. I’m not sure we will ever be the same again.”

Wilton then addressed Hall directly, adding: “You pretended to care for Sonia. You didn’t at all. You used her to fulfil your sick fantasies. You had her life in your hands. You had the opportunity to save her, but instead you preyed on her vulnerabilities and you took her from us.”

items.lbText:
Pro-Palestinian donor James ‘Fergie’ Chambers released as court considers extradition request

In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and his partner, Stella Schnabel, acting on a request from US authorities.

Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.

Speaking outside Madrid’s Aranjuez prison upon his release on Friday, Chambers called the charges against him “baseless”, adding that his release was “hopefully the first step in recognizing that internationally”.

Chambers also said: “Spain is a country that has stood on the right side of this most important issue of our time, that has stood on the right side of the genocide, and where this is some reason and some justice.”

An appeals court ordered the conditional release on Friday due to issues surrounding the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported on by the Guardian. He had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza.

The order asserts that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”.

Chambers’s release follows a separate decision on Thursday by the three-judge panel at the high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish.

The Guardian detailed four examples of the alterations on 7 November and the US admitted to tampering with the translation, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent” on 17 November – and citing the same four examples. Chambers’s defense team has asserted for weeks that there are as many as 30 such alterations.

The changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian earlier this week. The judges must consider the prosecutor’s report in deciding on the extradition request.

The high court was expected to rule on the extradition this week, following a 13 November hearing. But as of Thursday’s decision, the deadline has been extended indefinitely as the judges evaluate the translation, including a 345-page report submitted by the defense team that identifies 30 “incriminating changes” Trump administration officials made to a translation prepared by DeepL, “an AI-first translation platform”, according to its website .

The decision also gives the prosecutor an opportunity to address the issue in writing, after dismissing it in the 13 November hearing by referring to “supposed translation errors”.

Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”

The heir to $250m from his family’s business, Cox Enterprises, is being sought in extradition because of such views, his defense team has asserted throughout the case.

Meanwhile, the Irish Garda Síochána, acting on a request from US authorities, raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and Schnabel on Wednesday, destroying the front door and removing electronic items and other possessions, according to their attorney in Ireland , Ciarán Mulholland.

Schnabel, who is five months pregnant, said: “It is difficult to see this raid as anything other than a desperate fishing expedition by the US authorities to find evidence to bolster their case against Fergie.”

The attorney told the Guardian that the raid was the result of a “mutual legal assistance” request from the US – and that such a request “wouldn’t give [the Garda Síochána] permission to kick in the doors of someone’s dwelling in Ireland”.

“It’s unusual for the Irish state to be acting in such a clandestine manner,” Mulholland said. He has asked authorities to produce a search warrant and an itemized list of what was taken. “My fear is that whatever was taken has been put on a plane and taken to the US,” he added.

“This [extradition case] shows the complete disregard for due process … that the Trump administration seems to have,” Mulholland said.
